issues.failure_explanation: The 'if' direction fails at the degenerate choice C=D=0. There C+D=0 holds, but from the paper's own formulas G(z)=[1+z(1/6+(2/3)R(z))]/(1-z/6) with R(z)=1+24/z+O(1/z^2), so G(z) tends to (5z/6)/(-z/6)=-5 as z->infinity, not 0. The asymptotic ratio (C+D)/(C-D/2) is the indeterminate 0/0 at this point; the actual limit is -5, so the biconditional 'G(infinity)=0 iff C+D=0' is false at (C,D)=(0,0).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Exclude the degenerate point: state that G(infinity)=0 if and only if C+D=0 and (C,D)!=(0,0), noting that G(infinity)=-5 at C=D=0.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma 3.1 is false at the single degenerate parameter point (C,D)=(0,0). No downstream result uses that point (the final scheme takes D=-C with C>0), so no other claim is affected.
issues.title: Lemma 3.1 fails at the degenerate point C=D=0
issues.why_classification: Only a single degenerate parameter point is affected; a local exclusion repairs the biconditional with no loss to any substantive claim, method, or downstream result.

issues.failure_explanation: The asserted real part Re(z)=(1/3+13C)/(6C) is the mean of the two roots of (equation_C); it equals the real part of each root only when the roots are complex conjugates. For every C<=0 the discriminant (1/6+13C/2)^2-6C is strictly positive, so the roots are real, and their product 2/(3C) is negative, so exactly one root is negative. Hence for every C<0, including the entire branch C<-1/39 asserted in the lemma, G(z) has a pole in the open left half-plane and is not analytic in Re(z)<=0. Counterexample: C=-1 gives roots (38±sqrt(1660))/18, approximately 4.375 and -0.152. The correct necessary and sufficient condition is C>=0.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate Lemma 3.2 with the condition C>=0 only, replacing the single real-part formula by a case analysis of real versus complex-conjugate roots (for C<0 the roots are real with opposite signs, so one always lies in the left half-plane).
issues.overall_effect: Lemma 3.2 certifies analyticity (Condition 1) for a spurious half-line C<-1/39 of parameters; a scheme built with any such C actually has a pole of G in the left half-plane and is unstable. The paper's final A-stability conclusion is unaffected because it restricts to C>0.
issues.title: Lemma 3.2 wrongly certifies analyticity for the branch C < -1/39
issues.why_classification: The lemma asserts a false valid regime (a half-line of parameters), and the repair must redo the root-sign analysis and shrink the lemma's stated region - a limited weakening - although no downstream result relies on the false branch.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Analytically proving $\lvert G(iy)\lvert\leq 1$ for all $y\in\mathbb{R}$ is complex. Instead, we employ a systematic numerical scanning algorithm to determine the A-stability conditions of the scheme.

issues.failure_explanation: Condition 2 is never proven - the paper substitutes a finite numerical scan, which it concedes ('Analytically proving |G(iy)|<=1 ... is complex. Instead, we employ a systematic numerical scanning algorithm') - and the resulting interval is wrong. Substituting z=i (y=1) into the paper's own formulas gives R(i)=(2065+1128i)/2353, Re N=(1601+10992C)/2353, Im N=(10613-67719C)/14118, Re D=1-3C/2, Im D=-(1+39C)/6, and |G(i)|<=1 reduces to 65881647*C^2-4235400*C+56472<=0, i.e., C in [0.018875..., 0.045413...]. Both claimed endpoints violate this: the left-hand side equals +89.5 at C=0.018824 (|G(i)|^2=1+4.4e-7) and +309.9 at C=0.045589 (|G(i)|^2=1+1.4e-6). A-stability requires |G(iy)|<=1 for all real y, so the claimed interval is too wide at both ends: values in [0.018824, 0.018875) and (0.045413, 0.045589] are not A-stable (the binding violation occurs near y=1).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply the missing verification of Condition 2 (|G(iy)|^2<=1 reduces to non-negativity of a polynomial in y^2 with C-dependent coefficients) and restate Conclusion 3.3 and (Stage_2_final) with the corrected admissible interval (approximately [0.01888, 0.04541], the binding constraint occurring near y=1); alternatively downgrade the claim to numerically observed A-stability.
issues.overall_effect: The central stability guarantee - A-stability of the Implicit TSFO scheme for D=-C with C in [0.018824, 0.045589] (Conclusion 3.3), restated for the final scheme (Stage_2_final) and echoed in the abstract and conclusions - is not mathematically established and is false near both endpoints of the claimed interval. The recommended value C=0.018924 satisfies the y=1 constraint, so the numerical experiments remain admissible.
issues.title: A-stability interval in Conclusion 3.3 is unproven and false at both endpoints
issues.why_classification: A recognizably comparable result survives (A-stability on a nearly identical interval containing the recommended parameter C=0.018924), but the repair needs the contained yet nontrivial stability proof that was skipped plus a slight weakening of the advertised parameter range.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Additionally, a direct comparison is conducted between the proposed implicit TSFO scheme and the classical fourth-order implicit Runge-Kutta (e.g., Implicit RK4) method, focusing on stable time step size and convergence error, to verify the superiority of the former.
Comparisons with classical explicit and implicit fourth-order Runge-Kutta methods demonstrate that the proposed scheme possesses superior stability regions and smaller numerical errors.
$L^2$-Norm Error and Convergence Order Analysis of Implicit TSFO and Implicit RK4 Methods for "Linear Systems with Widely Separated Eigenvalues".

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that a comparison 'focusing on stable time step size' is conducted to verify the scheme's superiority over Implicit RK4, and asserts the scheme 'offers superior stability that enables even larger step sizes'. Section 5 contains only error and convergence-order tables at identical, stable step sizes; no stable-time-step or stability-region comparison is presented anywhere, so the stability-superiority claim is unsupported as written. Moreover, if the classical fourth-order implicit Runge-Kutta reference is A-stable (as the standard Gauss-type choice is), its stability region is the entire left half-plane and cannot be surpassed.

failure_location.quote: our scheme reduces the numerical error by about an order of magnitude under identical time steps and offers superior stability that enables even larger step sizes.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either present the promised stable-time-step / stability-region comparison or restrict the claims to what is demonstrated (smaller errors at identical stable step sizes).
issues.overall_effect: The stability-competitiveness claims (end of Section 5 and the Conclusions' 'superior stability regions') are not backed by any presented experiment; only the smaller-error-at-identical-step-size comparison is supported.
issues.title: Stability superiority over implicit RK4 claimed but never demonstrated
issues.why_classification: A local prose correction (delete or substantiate the superiority claim); no formal result, scheme, or computation is affected.
